Bright or saturated colour palettes — no electric blues, neon greens, or startup-gradient aesthetics
Rounded, playful, or cartoon-style design elements
Literal leopard or animal imagery — the brand metaphor is applied through language, not visuals
Generic AI imagery — no glowing brains, robot faces, or neural network clichés
Cluttered layouts or dense information grids without breathing room
Decorative animations or parallax effects that slow page load
Testimonial carousels or social proof widgets without real attributed content
Cookie-cutter SaaS landing page patterns with floating screenshots
Any visual element that a generalist digital agency would produce for a non-technical audience
data.colour_mood: Deep charcoal and near-black backgrounds with warm amber, gold, and copper accents. This palette signals premium technical authority — the dark foundation conveys engineering seriousness and production infrastructure depth, while the amber-gold accents reference the leopardess brand (speed, warmth, precision) without being literal. Secondary colours: muted warm greys for body text, subtle copper for hover states and interactive elements. Code blocks and technical references in a slightly lighter charcoal with amber syntax highlighting. The overall mood is: 'This is infrastructure you can trust, built by people who ship.'
data.typography_mood: Primary headings in a geometric sans-serif with medium weight and generous tracking — think Inter, Geist, or similar engineering-grade typefaces. Body text in a highly legible sans-serif at comfortable reading size (18px+) with relaxed line-height for technical content scanning. Monospace font for any code references, agent names, or infrastructure terms to signal technical authenticity. The typography should feel like developer documentation meets premium consultancy — precise, scannable, and never decorative.
data.imagery_direction: All imagery should be abstract technical visualizations — no stock photography of people in offices, no handshakes, no generic AI brain imagery. Every image should suggest real infrastructure: distributed systems, orchestration flows, data pipelines, hierarchical agent coordination. The visual language should make a CTO feel they are looking at a company that builds actual systems. Subtle references to Kubernetes pod topology, Kafka partition layouts, and state machine workflows are welcome. Dark backgrounds throughout with amber-gold accent lighting.
data.layout_preference: Clean, spacious layouts with generous whitespace and strong vertical rhythm. Content sections should breathe — no cramped grids. Technical content gets full-width treatment with clear visual hierarchy. Service cards and case study cards use consistent grid layouts (3-column on desktop, stacking cleanly on mobile). Hero sections are tall and impactful with a single clear message. CTAs are prominent but not aggressive — the audience responds to specificity, not urgency. Navigation is minimal and functional. The overall layout should feel like a well-architected system: everything has its place, nothing is redundant.

use_cases.title: Production Agent Orchestration, Built and Delivered
use_cases.results: Production agent infrastructure delivered on proven stack. Runs unattended for weeks, pauses for human input when configured to.
use_cases.summary: You need agents that run reliably in production — not a framework that works in demos. I build the orchestration layer on Kubernetes, Kafka, and Postgres: workflow-driven agents with proper state management, timeout recovery, and horizontal scaling. Human review gates are configurable per workflow stage — fully autonomous where you're confident, human-in-the-loop where you're not. The system runs thousands of agent instances in production today.

use_cases.title: Multi-Stage Pipelines with Configurable Human Oversight
use_cases.client: Teams Needing Automated Content or Data Pipelines
use_cases.results: Autonomous pipelines that handle the volume while your team handles the judgment calls.
use_cases.summary: You have a pipeline problem: collecting data from multiple sources, validating it against authoritative records, transforming it, and publishing — and right now too much of that is manual. I build agent pipelines where each stage runs independently with its own error handling and retry logic. Every stage can be set to autonomous or human-approval, independently. Your team reviews what matters and lets the rest flow.

use_cases.title: Problem-First Assessment and Implementation
use_cases.client: Engineering Teams Evaluating AI for Their Operations
use_cases.results: An honest technical assessment followed by delivery. No predetermined solution — the recommendation fits the problem.
use_cases.summary: You describe the problem — whether that's operational bottlenecks, data quality issues, or scaling challenges. I research your domain, your constraints, and what's been tried. Then I propose something specific: sometimes that's an agent system, sometimes it's infrastructure, sometimes it's a workflow change that doesn't need AI at all. I build what we agree on, with your team having visibility and approval at every step.

use_cases.title: Continuous Quality Improvement Pipeline
use_cases.client: Businesses with Deployed Systems That Need Ongoing Improvement
use_cases.results: Systems that improve autonomously between human review cycles. Routine maintenance handled, significant issues escalated with full context.
use_cases.summary: Your site or platform is live but quality degrades over time — content goes stale, tools break, new gaps appear. I build improvement loops that run continuously: content audits, tool health checks, structural analysis, and automated fixes. Each finding is classified by severity and routed appropriately — automated fixes for routine issues, human review for anything that needs judgment. The system gets smarter about your specific quality standards over time.

case_studies.title: Hierarchical Agent Architecture for Autonomous Website Operations
case_studies.results: Six production sites deployed and self-maintaining. Stateless agent pods scale horizontally with zero-downtime workflow updates via database configuration. Full observability through processing history, error routing, and orchestration audit trails.
case_studies.summary: Designed and delivered a production agent orchestration platform running on Kubernetes, Kafka, and Postgres. Over 30 specialised agent types coordinate through hierarchical workflows — from domain research through content generation, design, tool deployment, and ongoing quality improvement. The system deploys complete websites from a domain name input and maintains them autonomously.

case_studies.title: Multi-Stage Data Pipeline with Companies House Verification
case_studies.results: Thousands of verified business records with financial enrichment. Automated matching cascade handles name variations, dissolved companies, and registration gaps without manual intervention.
case_studies.summary: Built a structured data collection pipeline spanning area discovery, entity scraping, and automated business verification against Companies House. Each pipeline stage operates as independent agents with their own error handling and retry logic, coordinated through work items and Kafka messaging.

case_studies.title: Real-Time Multi-Source News Pipeline with Credibility Scoring
case_studies.results: Four ingestion source types operational with automated credibility classification. Production deployment with six-hour refresh cycles and source health monitoring.
case_studies.summary: Delivered a content feed system ingesting from RSS, news search APIs, and the xAI Responses API. An LLM-powered triage agent scores relevance and credibility per item, tracking provenance from original publisher through discovery channel. Rendered output commits via GitHub Actions to Cloudflare-hosted sites.

case_studies.title: LLM-Driven Tool Generation and Deployment Pipeline
case_studies.results: End-to-end autonomous tool lifecycle: evaluation, generation, deployment, content integration, and quality auditing. Tools deployed across multiple verticals with industry-appropriate suggestions and zero manual development.
case_studies.summary: Engineered an autonomous pipeline where an LLM evaluates what interactive tools benefit a site's specific audience, generates self-contained HTML/CSS/JS tools, deploys them with navigation entries and companion guides, then creates cross-references from related content pages — closing the loop between tool creation and content integration.

data.tone: Authoritative-technical throughout. All copy — including CTAs, hero text, about page, and microcopy — should address senior engineering and technical leadership directly. Language should reflect production credibility and system depth. Avoid casual phrases ('Work Smarter, Not Harder'), motivational filler, or SMB-oriented softening language. CTAs should be action-specific and technically grounded (e.g. 'Review the Architecture', 'See How We Deploy', 'Start a Technical Conversation') rather than generic or inspirational. The voice is that of a senior engineer who also understands business outcomes — precise, confident, and free of consultant clichés.
data.content_voice: Content voice is anchored in the leopardess brand metaphor: precision, agility, speed, and stealth. These are not decorative — they map directly to engineering outcomes. Precision = deterministic agent behaviour, typed contracts, observable pipelines. Agility = iterative delivery cadence, composable architecture, fast feedback loops. Speed = time-to-production measured in days, not sprints. Stealth = low operational overhead, systems that run quietly without constant human intervention. Headlines and body copy should use this vocabulary to describe specific technical outcomes rather than generic transformation language. Banned phrases: 'digital transformation', 'production-ready' (unless followed by a specific stack qualifier), 'days not months' (unless paired with a concrete delivery example), 'AI-powered' (unqualified). Preferred framing: name the problem, name the system that solves it, name the outcome. Example rewrite — instead of 'production-ready AI systems delivered in days not months', prefer 'orchestrated agent pipelines on Kubernetes, scoped and deployed within a two-week engagement'. The primary audience evaluates vendors on specificity; vague benefit language signals low credibility to CTOs and engineering leads.
data.tone_and_register: All copy must maintain a single consistent register: technically precise, direct, and credible. Brand language ('Grace and Precision', 'Leopardess') is permitted as a framing device but must always resolve into a concrete technical or delivery claim within the same sentence or paragraph. Brand metaphors must never stand alone or substitute for specificity. The pattern is: brand framing → technical substance, not brand framing → benefit language. Example: 'Grace and Precision means your orchestration layer handles failover without manual intervention — not that we care deeply about your outcomes.' Aspirational or poetic phrasing that is not immediately grounded in a system behaviour, stack component, or delivery outcome should be removed or rewritten. This applies to all pages including index, about, and services.
data.cta_copy_governance: CTA copy must be differentiated by the visitor's likely intent stage. Index page CTAs address awareness-stage visitors: lead with the problem being solved (engineering teams wasting cycles on AI systems that never reach production), not the solution. Services page CTAs address evaluation-stage visitors: lead with what makes the delivery approach distinctive (specific infrastructure choices, hierarchical agent model, human oversight configurability, delivery speed without reliability trade-offs). The phrase 'actually ships' or 'AI agents that actually ship' is retired from all locations except one canonical placement — currently the about page H2 — and must not appear in CTA headlines, hero subheadings, or services page copy. Any new CTA written for any page must first identify the visitor's stage (awareness, evaluation, decision) and write to that stage exclusively. Repetition of motifs across pages signals content shallowness to a technical reader who visits more than one page; each CTA should be independently persuasive without relying on accumulated repetition.
data.tone_and_audience_targeting: Primary audience is CTOs, engineering leads, and technical founders at UK scale-ups and B2B SaaS companies. All CTAs, hero copy, and section headlines must use technical-credibility language consistent with this audience. Phrases like 'Work Smarter, Not Harder', 'Get started in minutes', or other SMB-accessible idioms are out of scope and should be replaced with language that signals production depth, engineering rigour, and measurable outcomes (e.g. 'Deploy your first agent pipeline in a single sprint', 'Built on Kubernetes, Kafka, and Postgres — not wrappers'). Non-technical SMB buyers are explicitly out of scope and no page should contain copy that targets or accommodates them. Where a page currently mixes tones, the technical-enterprise register takes precedence and accessible language should be removed or rewritten.

data.site_brief: Industry: AI consulting and agent orchestration (technology services). Primary audience: Three personas — (1) CTOs and engineering leads at UK scale-ups (50–500 employees) who need proof of production deployments and working code, not slide decks; (2) Founders of B2B SaaS or professional services firms who are technically literate, lack an internal AI/ML team, and need a delivery partner who can own end-to-end build; (3) Operations and transformation leads at mid-market UK businesses seeking practical automation of high-volume workflows without hiring a full data engineering team. All three personas are time-poor, results-driven, and respond to specificity, working demos, and clear ROI framing. Tone: Practical, direct, technically credible — the voice of engineers who build real systems, not consultants who produce reports. Conversion purpose: Generate qualified inbound leads and demo requests from UK businesses ready to commission AI agent or automation work, with a secondary goal of establishing technical authority through case studies, tools, and insights content.

data.brand_voice_guidelines: The Leopardess name is a live brand asset and should be referenced naturally at least once per page through metaphor rather than explicit explanation. The leopardess archetype carries: speed (fast delivery, rapid iteration, no slow consulting cycles), precision (targeted solutions, no wasted motion, surgical automation), adaptability (hunts in complex terrain, works across stacks and sectors), and instinct (pattern recognition, knowing where to move before the client does). Apply these qualities to describe how the team works, how systems are built, and how problems are approached. Examples: 'We move fast because we've already mapped the terrain', 'precision-built agents, not broad-brush automation', 'we don't advise from the sidelines — we hunt the problem alongside you'. Avoid forced or literal animal references. The metaphor should feel like a natural extension of the practical-expert voice, not a mascot gimmick.
